turns.t: Come in, Mr Thackeray, have a seat. I've got the letter from your last visit here, where you were worried about your hand. How have things been since then?
Well, doctor, you know, the hand is still doing it. It was a Tuesday when I wrote to you. No, a Wednesday, the bins had gone out.
So the hand is still doing it. Which hand, and what does it do?
My right one. It shakes when I'm sitting with it in my lap, watching the television, and then it stops when I pick up the paper. Or is it the left? No, right, definitely right.
Right hand, shaking at rest, and it settles when you use it. That's useful to know. How long has it been going on?
Four months. No, five. My daughter says six months, and she keeps a diary, so we'll say six months.
Six months, then. And you mentioned in the letter that your family have noticed something else as well?
Yes, my daughter says I'm walking slower. I think I'm walking at the same speed, but she says that when we go to the shops I'm always three paces behind her.
So your walking has got slower, at least in her eyes. Do you notice it yourself at all?
A bit, going up the road to the post box. I used to do it in five minutes and now it's more like ten, and I do have to stop for a breath.
Thank you. Now I need to ask, have you had any falls?
No, no falls. A stumble on the kerb once, but I caught myself on the lamppost. No falls.
Good. So no falls, just a stumble you caught yourself from. What medicines do you take at the moment?
Just the one, ramipril, 5 mg once a day, for the blood pressure. I put it next to the kettle so I don't forget it.
Ramipril, 5 mg once a day. Any other tablets, even over the counter?
No, only that. Oh, and I'm to avoid codeine. I was allergic to it years ago, made me violently sick, and I've never touched it since.
Thank you, I'll note that you had a bad reaction to codeine. Now, tell me a little about home. Who's there with you?
I live alone in a bungalow, since my wife passed. The daughter comes on Sundays. I smoked thirty a day till 1989, then I gave it up overnight.
So you live alone and you stopped smoking in 1989. Well done on that, it's not easy. Any other conditions I should have on my list, besides the high blood pressure?
Just the blood pressure, since I was about fifty. And the hearing, I've got hearing loss, you'll have to speak up a bit, doctor.
I'll speak up. High blood pressure and hearing loss. Let me do your numbers now and then look at your arm and watch you walk.
Which arm do you want?
Your left for the cuff, please. Your blood pressure is 146 over 84, pulse 72 bpm, oxygen saturation 97 %, temperature 36.6 °C and you weigh 69 kg.
Is that good? It sounds like a lot of numbers.
Nothing alarming. The pressure is a touch up, but we'll not chase that today. Now, give me your right arm, let me bend your elbow slowly. Relax it completely.
I'm trying. It wants to hold on.
I can feel cogwheel rigidity in your right arm, a ratchet-like stiffness as I move it. Now, stand up and walk to the door and back for me.
You've got reduced arm swing when you walk, mostly on the right, and your steps are small. Sit down again, you did well.
Small steps? I thought I was doing marvellously.
You were, you were. Let me say back what I've found. A shake in the right hand at rest, slower walking, stiffness in the right arm, and less swing as you walk. Together that points one way.
Which way is that?
Most likely early Parkinson's disease. That's my provisional view, not a final answer, and it's a condition we can manage well for many years.
Parkinson's. Right. I've read a bit about it in the paper, and none of it was cheerful.
It varies enormously from person to person, and yours looks mild. Please don't picture the worst version of it.
I'll try not to. What happens now?
I'd like to arrange a blood test today, to check a few other things that can mimic this, and then I'll see you again in six weeks to go through it.
In six weeks. I'll put it on the calendar by the kettle, with the pills.
Perfect. Blood test today, and back here in six weeks. Take care on the way out, Mr Thackeray.
